title: Kong Yiji
subtitle: Lu Xun (1919) — a failed scholar in a dirty gown, a tavern that laughs at him, and a boy who warms the wine and remembers.
crosslink: Need an easier version? Read this story at A2/B1 level →
intention: you'll tell the story of a man whose whole life is a contradiction — a scholar who steals, a gentleman who stands with the labourers — and use the language of contrast and concession: although, even though, despite, yet, for all his…
warmup: Think of a person everybody in a town, office or school laughed at. Why them? Did anyone ever stop?
Is education worth anything if it never leads to a job or a position? What does it give — and what can it take away?
A debt of nineteen coins, written on a board. What is the smallest thing you have ever seen a person remembered by?
vocab_intro: Before we read, let's unlock the words you'll need. Think first — the Reveal only confirms.

vocab.heading: A. Work it out from the sentence
vocab.instruction: Read each sentence aloud and say what the bold word means from the rest of the sentence. Then reveal.

items.sent: The tavern had a counter facing the street where working men stood to drink a bowl of warm wine before going home.
items.meaning: a tavern (n) — an inn or bar where drink (and simple food) is sold.

items.sent: He was so pedantic that he corrected the boy's handwriting and then told him there were four ways to write the character — as if anyone needed to know.
items.meaning: pedantic (adj) — too concerned with small details or rules of learning; showing off knowledge. (n: a pedant)

items.sent: He was not a robber; he pilfered — a book here, a brush and inkstone there — small things from people who had trusted him.
items.meaning: to pilfer (v) — to steal small things, especially repeatedly.

items.sent: The last time they saw him he was a wretched sight: thin, black-faced, dragging himself along on his hands.
items.meaning: wretched (adj) — in a very unhappy or pitiful state; miserable.

vocab.heading: B. From the meaning to the word
vocab.instruction: Which word fits the definition? The first letter is given. Say the word, then reveal.

items.sent: A learned person, someone who has studied the classics — in old China, the class that wore long gowns and sat down to drink. It begins with s.
items.meaning: a scholar (n) — a person of learning. In this story, a would-be scholar who never passed the imperial examinations.

items.sent: To laugh at someone in a cruel way, to make them look foolish in public. It begins with r.
items.meaning: to ridicule (v) / ridicule (n) — to mock; cruel laughter at someone's expense.

items.sent: The quality of deserving respect; self-respect that survives poverty or insult. It begins with d.
items.meaning: dignity (n) — a calm, serious manner that deserves respect; self-respect.

vocab.heading: C. Complete the chunk
vocab.instruction: These words live inside fixed phrases. Say the missing word, then reveal.

items.sent: Nobody else at the tavern paid on time, but Kong Yiji never left a debt for long: whatever was chalked up on the ___, he cleared within the month.
items.meaning: the slate (n) — the board on which a customer's debts are written; to run up a debt on the slate, to wipe the slate clean.

items.sent: His eyes seemed to ___ with the landlord not to mention it again — no words, just a look.
items.meaning: to plead with someone — to beg earnestly. He pleaded with them for mercy.

items.sent: Only Kong Yiji stood at the ___ in a long gown; the other gowned customers sat inside.
items.meaning: the counter (n) — the long table across which drinks are served; to stand at the counter, over the counter.

vocab_use: Sort the ten words into the tavern, Kong Yiji himself and what the others do to him. Say why.
Using scholar, pilfer and ridicule, guess what kind of man this story is about — and how it ends.
story_intro: Lu Xun's story, translated here from the Chinese and only lightly shortened. It is told by a boy who worked in the tavern, remembering twenty years later. Read each part; after it, try the quick check from memory, then talk about the question.

story.title: Part 1 — The man who stood at the counter in a long gown
paras: The taverns of Luzhen are laid out differently from anywhere else: each has a big L-shaped counter facing the street, with hot water kept ready behind it so that wine can be warmed at any hour. Working men, when they knock off at noon or dusk, spend four coppers on a bowl of wine — that was twenty years ago; a bowl costs ten now — and drink it hot, standing outside the counter, to rest. For a copper more they can buy a saucer of salted bamboo shoots or aniseed beans to go with it; for a dozen or so, a meat dish. But these customers are mostly of the short-jacket class and seldom so extravagant. Only the men in long gowns stroll into the room beside the shop, order wine and food, and sit down to drink at their leisure.

From the age of twelve I worked as a boy in the Xianheng tavern at the edge of town. The landlord said I looked too simple to serve the long-gowned customers, so I was to work outside. The short-jacket customers outside were easier to talk to, but many of them were fussy and hard to please. They liked to watch the yellow wine ladled out of the jar with their own eyes, to check there was no water at the bottom of the jug, and to see the jug put into the hot water themselves before they were satisfied; under such strict supervision, watering the wine was very hard. So after a few days the landlord said I was no good at that either. Luckily the man who had recommended me carried some weight, so I could not be dismissed, and I was given the dull job of warming wine and nothing else.

From then on I stood all day behind the counter attending to my duty. I did nothing wrong, but I found it monotonous and rather pointless. The landlord had a fierce face and the customers had no kind words, so there was no way to be cheerful; only when Kong Yiji came to the tavern could I laugh a little. That is why I remember him still.

Kong Yiji was the only man who stood to drink and wore a long gown. He was tall and big, with a pale face on which the wrinkles were often crossed with scars, and a tangled, greying beard. He wore a long gown, true, but it was dirty and torn, and looked as if it had not been mended or washed for over ten years. When he spoke to people his mouth was full of classical phrases — 'verily' and 'forsooth' — that nobody quite understood. Because his surname was Kong, people gave him a nickname out of the half-nonsense line in the children's copybook, 'Kong Yiji, the great man above', and Kong Yiji he became. The moment he arrived, every drinker looked at him and laughed, and someone would shout: 'Kong Yiji, you've got a new scar on your face!' He would not answer; he would say to the counter, 'Warm two bowls of wine, and a dish of aniseed beans,' and lay out nine coppers in a row. Then they would shout, deliberately loud: 'You've been stealing again!' Kong Yiji would open his eyes wide: 'How can you blacken a man's good name out of nothing…' 'Good name? I saw you with my own eyes the day before yesterday, stealing books from the He family, and strung up and beaten for it.' Then Kong Yiji would flush red, the veins standing out on his forehead, and protest: 'Taking books can't be counted as stealing… taking books! … a scholar's business — can that be called stealing?' There would follow a string of hard-to-understand phrases — 'the gentleman keeps his integrity in poverty' and the like — until the whole company roared with laughter, and inside and outside the shop the air was full of cheerfulness.

check.q: What is the difference between the short-jacket customers and the long-gowned ones — and where does Kong Yiji fit?
check.a: Short jackets are working men who drink standing at the counter for four coppers; long gowns are gentlemen who sit inside and order food. Kong Yiji is the only man who wears a long gown — dirty and torn — and stands outside to drink with the labourers.

check.q: What is his answer when the drinkers accuse him of stealing books?
check.a: That 'taking books can't be counted as stealing' — it is 'a scholar's business' — followed by classical phrases nobody understands, until the whole tavern laughs.

story.discuss: 'Only when Kong Yiji came could I laugh a little. That is why I remember him still.' The narrator's only fond memory of the tavern is a man being humiliated. What does that tell you about the tavern — and about the narrator?

story.title: Part 2 — 'Do you know there are four ways to write it?'
paras: From what people said behind his back, Kong Yiji had studied, but had never passed the examinations, and had no way of making a living; so he grew poorer and poorer until he was nearly a beggar. Fortunately he wrote a fine hand, and could copy books for people in exchange for a bowl of rice. Unfortunately he had a bad habit too: he liked to drink and hated to work. After a few days at a job, man, books, paper, brushes and inkstone would all vanish together. After this had happened several times, nobody asked him to copy any more. Kong Yiji had no way out, and now and then could not help pilfering. But in our tavern his conduct was better than anyone's: he never failed to pay. Sometimes, when he had no ready money, his name went up on the slate for a while; but within a month he always cleared it, and his name was wiped off.

After half a bowl of wine, when the red had faded from his face, the others would start again: 'Kong Yiji, can you really read?' He would look at the questioner with an air of disdain, as if the question were beneath an answer. Then they would go on: 'So how is it you never got even half a degree?' At once Kong Yiji would look crushed and uneasy, and a grey colour would come over his face, and he would mutter something; this time it was all 'verily' and 'forsooth', and nobody understood a word. And again the whole company would roar with laughter, and inside and outside the shop the air was full of cheerfulness.

At such times I could join in the laughter without the landlord scolding me; indeed, the landlord himself always put the same questions to Kong Yiji to make people laugh. Kong Yiji knew he could not talk with them, so he had no choice but to talk to the children. Once he said to me: 'Have you been to school?' I nodded slightly. 'Been to school… then I'll test you. The hui in aniseed beans — how do you write it?' I thought: does a man little better than a beggar have any business testing me? — and turned my face away and ignored him. Kong Yiji waited a long while, then said very earnestly: 'You can't write it? … I'll teach you. Remember it! These characters ought to be remembered. When you're a landlord yourself, you'll need them for the accounts.' I thought to myself that I was still a very long way from being a landlord, and that our landlord never entered aniseed beans in the accounts anyway; and, half amused and half impatient, I answered lazily: 'Who wants you to teach me? Isn't it the hui with grass on top and a box underneath?' Kong Yiji looked delighted, tapped two long fingernails on the counter, and nodded: 'Right, right! … Did you know there are four ways of writing hui?' I grew still more impatient, pursed my lips and walked away. Kong Yiji had just dipped a nail in his wine to write on the counter; seeing my complete lack of interest, he sighed again and looked deeply sorry.

Sometimes the children of the neighbourhood, hearing the laughter, came running to join the fun and crowded round him. He would give them aniseed beans, one each. When they had eaten the beans they did not go away, but kept their eyes on the dish. Kong Yiji would grow flustered, spread his five fingers over the dish, and bend down to say: 'There aren't many left. I haven't many left.' Then he would straighten up, look at the beans again, and shake his head: 'Not many, not many! Are they many? Nay, they are not many.' And the whole flock of children would scatter, laughing.
That was how Kong Yiji made people cheerful. But without him, other people got along just the same.

check.q: How did Kong Yiji come to be so poor, and what was the one thing he did better than anyone in the tavern?
check.a: He studied but never passed the examinations, could not make a living, and lost his copying jobs by drinking and disappearing with the books and brushes; so he pilfered. Yet he always paid his debts — his name never stayed on the slate more than a month.

check.q: What does he try to teach the boy, and how does the boy respond?
check.a: How to write the character hui in 'aniseed beans' — and that it has four forms. The boy thinks a near-beggar has no business testing him, answers lazily and walks off; Kong Yiji sighs, looking deeply sorry.

story.discuss: 'Are they many? Nay, they are not many.' The children laugh; so does the reader. But what is he protecting with his five fingers over that dish — and what is Lu Xun protecting him from, by letting us laugh?

story.title: Part 3 — Nineteen coppers
paras: One day, two or three days before the Mid-Autumn Festival, the landlord was slowly making up the accounts, and took down the slate, and suddenly said: 'Kong Yiji hasn't been in for a long time. He still owes nineteen coppers!' Only then did I realise that it really was a long time since he had come. One of the drinkers said: 'How could he come? … They've broken his legs.' 'Oh!' said the landlord. 'He was stealing again. This time he must have lost his head — he went and stole from the Ding family, the provincial graduate. Can you steal from a house like that?' 'And then?' 'And then? First they made him write a confession, then they beat him — beat him half the night, and then broke his legs.' 'And after that?' 'After that, his legs were broken.' 'And with his legs broken?' 'What then? … Who knows? Perhaps he's dead.' The landlord asked no more, and went on slowly with his accounts.

After the Mid-Autumn Festival the autumn wind grew colder every day, and it was nearly the start of winter; even standing all day by the fire I had to wear my padded jacket. One afternoon, when there was not a single customer, I was sitting with my eyes closed when I suddenly heard a voice: 'Warm a bowl of wine.' It was very low, but very familiar. I looked, and there was nobody. I stood up and looked out over the counter — and there was Kong Yiji, sitting on the ground below the counter facing the doorstep. His face was dark and thin and no longer looked like a face; he wore a ragged lined jacket, sat cross-legged on a straw mat slung from his shoulders by a rope, and, seeing me, said again: 'Warm a bowl of wine.' The landlord leaned out too. 'Kong Yiji? You still owe nineteen coppers!' Kong Yiji looked up wretchedly and answered: 'That… I'll settle it next time. This time I've cash. Let the wine be good.' The landlord said, laughing, just as he always had: 'Kong Yiji, you've been stealing again!' But this time he did not argue much; he said only, 'Don't make fun of me.' 'Make fun? If you hadn't been stealing, how did your legs get broken?' Kong Yiji said in a low voice: 'A fall. I fell, fell…' and his eyes seemed to plead with the landlord not to mention it again. By now several people had gathered, and they laughed with the landlord. I warmed the wine, carried it out and set it on the doorstep. He fumbled in his ragged pocket for four coppers and put them in my hand, and I saw that his hand was covered in mud — he had walked here on those hands. Before long he had finished the wine, and then, amid the laughter and talk of the others, he went slowly away, sitting, on those hands.

After that it was a long time before I saw Kong Yiji again. At the end of the year the landlord took down the slate and said: 'Kong Yiji still owes nineteen coppers!' At the Dragon Boat Festival the next year he said again: 'Kong Yiji still owes nineteen coppers!' But at the Mid-Autumn Festival he did not say it; and by the end of the year there was still no sign of him.
To this day I have never seen him again — so Kong Yiji is probably dead.

check.q: How does the tavern learn what happened to Kong Yiji, and how does the landlord react?
check.a: From a drinker, in a flat exchange: he stole from the Ding family, a graduate's house, was made to write a confession, beaten half the night, and his legs were broken. The landlord says 'Oh!' and goes back to his accounts.

check.q: Describe Kong Yiji's last visit — what he pays with, and what the landlord says.
check.a: He arrives sitting on a straw mat, dragging himself on his hands, dark and thin, and asks for a bowl of wine. The landlord reminds him of the nineteen coppers and jokes that he's been stealing again; Kong Yiji says he fell, pleads with his eyes, pays four muddy coppers, drinks, and goes away on his hands while the others laugh.

story.discuss: The landlord mentions the nineteen coppers at the New Year and again at the Dragon Boat Festival — then stops. The story ends 'probably dead'. Why does Lu Xun make the debt the only record of a man's life?

grammar.h2: The grammar this story runs on: contrast and concession
grammar.intro: Kong Yiji is a walking contradiction: a scholar who cannot earn a bowl of rice, a thief who always pays his debts, a man in a gentleman's gown who stands with the labourers. To talk about him you need the grammar that holds two opposite things in one sentence.
notes:
1. although / even though / though + clause.
• "Although he wore a long gown, he stood outside to drink." • "Even though he stole, he always paid his bill." (even though = stronger)
• though can also come at the end, informally: "He always paid, though."

2. despite / in spite of + noun or -ing (never a clause).
• "Despite his learning, he never passed." • "In spite of being a scholar, he was nearly a beggar."
• With a clause, add the fact that: "despite the fact that he could read…" ✗ despite he could read.

3. Other tools.
• yet / and yet — joins two sentences: "He was ridiculed daily; and yet he came back."
• for all + noun: "For all his classical phrases, he could not write an account."
• whereas / while — a contrast between two people or things: "The gowned customers sat inside, whereas Kong Yiji stood at the counter."

exercises.instruction: One each, from: although · despite · yet · for all · whereas. The grammar after the gap tells you which fits.
items: ___ his fine handwriting, nobody would give him copying work.
___ he stole from his employers, he never owed the tavern for more than a month.
The working men paid four coppers and stood, ___ the gentlemen sat inside and ordered food.
He was beaten, laughed at and forgotten; ___ he came back one more time for a bowl of wine.
___ his talk of 'the gentleman in poverty', he could not keep a job for a week.

exercises.h3: Rewrite with the connector in brackets
exercises.instruction: Keep the meaning; change the structure. Watch what follows despite.
items: He had studied for years, but he never passed the examination. (despite)
He was a thief. He paid his debts. (even though)
He wore a gown. He stood with the labourers. (in spite of the fact that)
The landlord laughed at him. The landlord let him drink on credit. (and yet)
He had learning. He could not earn a bowl of rice. (for all)
answers: Despite (his) years of study / Despite having studied for years, he never passed the examination.
Even though he was a thief, he paid his debts.
In spite of the fact that he wore a gown, he stood with the labourers.
The landlord laughed at him, and yet he let him drink on credit.
For all his learning, he could not earn a bowl of rice.

exercises.h3: Put it together — a man in one paragraph
exercises.instruction: Fill each gap with the connector the hint asks for. Read it aloud.
items: ___ (although) he had read the classics, Kong Yiji never gained a degree; ___ (despite) his learning, he was nearly a beggar. He stole, ___ (yet) he was the only customer who always paid. The gentlemen sat inside, ___ (whereas) he stood at the counter in a torn gown. ___ (for all) the laughter, the boy remembers him twenty years on — ___ (even though) he never once stopped laughing himself.
answers: Although · despite · yet · whereas · For all · even though

grammar.outro: In the Speak tab you'll describe a man whose every quality has an opposite — and you'll need a concession in almost every sentence.

deeper.h2: Why this story stays with you
paras: Lu Xun (1881–1936) trained as a doctor in Japan and gave it up, he said, because the Chinese did not need their bodies cured so much as their spirit. 'Kong Yiji' was published in April 1919, weeks before the student protests that began modern China, in the magazine that led them; Lu Xun later said it was his own favourite among his stories. The imperial examinations that Kong Yiji failed — the only road to office for a thousand years, and the reason a man wore a long gown — had been abolished in 1905. He is a relic of a system that had already died, still wearing its uniform.

The cruelty of the story is in its cheerfulness. Nobody hates Kong Yiji; they enjoy him. The landlord's questions, the drinkers' shouts, the children's laughter and, above all, the boy who tells the story and joins in — 'without the landlord scolding me' — are all part of the same warm air 'inside and outside the shop'. Lu Xun called this the spectator's disease: a whole society watching suffering as entertainment. Kong Yiji's one uncorrupted virtue is that he pays his debts; his one act of kindness is to try to teach a bored child a character; and the only trace he leaves is nineteen coppers on a slate, read aloud twice and then not at all.
deeper.note: Look again at the four coppers. On his last visit he pays cash — 'this time I've cash' — with a hand covered in the mud he has crawled through. Why does Lu Xun make him insist on paying? What is the story saying about dignity and about money?
questions: The narrator is a boy who found the tavern 'monotonous' and could only laugh when Kong Yiji came. Twenty years later he writes this. Is the story a confession? Does he understand what he did?
'Taking books can't be counted as stealing.' Is this the excuse of a thief, the logic of a man who believes in learning, or both? Why books?
The landlord is not cruel — he is 'just as he always was'. Is habit crueller than malice? Who in the story is responsible for anything?
Lu Xun wanted to cure a nation's spirit. What does this story diagnose, and does the diagnosis apply beyond China, beyond 1919?

speak.useful: Holding opposites together: "Although he…, he…", "Despite his…, …", "…and yet…", "For all his…, …", "…whereas…". For opinions: "What's striking is…", "You could argue that…", "On one level… but on another…".

tasks.label: Task A · Tell the whole story (4 minutes)
paras: Tell 'Kong Yiji' to someone who has never read it. Move through the arc: the tavern and its two classes of customer → the man in the torn gown → 'taking books isn't stealing' → the copying jobs, the slate → the four ways to write hui → the aniseed beans → the broken legs → the last bowl of wine → nineteen coppers.
Use contrast and concession in almost every sentence about him, and at least five key words (tavern, pedantic, pilfer, wretched, scholar, ridicule, dignity, slate, plead, counter).

tasks.label: Task B · The trial of the tavern (4 minutes)
paras: Who is responsible for Kong Yiji: the examination system, the Ding family who broke his legs, the landlord, the drinkers, the boy — or Kong Yiji himself? Make the case against one of them, using concessions to admit what can be said in their defence. Then switch to a different defendant for one minute.

tasks.label: Task C · A person everyone laughed at (4 minutes)
paras: Describe a person — real, famous, or invented — who was the entertainment of a place: what people laughed at, what the laughter hid, and what became of them. Use contrast and concession to hold their dignity and their absurdity in the same sentence.
menu: The office eccentric whose jokes were repeated for years after redundancy.
A teacher the whole school imitated — and what you learned about them later.
A politician, comedian or reality-TV figure the public loved to mock.
A character from a novel or film: Don Quixote, Willy Loman, a Dickens clerk.
The village 'character' in the place your family comes from.
Someone who tried to teach you something you refused to learn.

final: 'Without him, other people got along just the same.' Is that the saddest sentence in the story, or simply true? Which people are 'necessary'?
The boy laughs, and remembers, and writes it down. Is remembering enough?
Kong Yiji insists on paying four coppers with a muddy hand. Is dignity something you keep, or something others allow you?
Before you go — from memory: three sentences about Kong Yiji, one with although, one with despite + noun, one with and yet.
